source_read: PMC full text PMC1976310 (Subst Abuse Treat Prev Policy 2007;2:25), read in the app's browser in my own tab; whole article read (abstract, Background, Methods, Results, Table 1 with its four footnotes, Discussion, Conclusion, competing interests, contributions, acknowledgements with the funding statement, reference list). The paper has no figures and no supplement. Card check only (the task lists no claims). I read the source and noted my own observations before opening the card, then recomputed every Table 1 percentage and total, the card's Wilson and Newcombe intervals, and all 10 two-group p-values (Fisher's exact and chi-square, with and without continuity correction).

key_findings.correction: 38, 21 and 11 of 70 are 54.3%, 30.0% and 15.7%; the Results sentence says half were in np-SAD's drug abuser/dependent category, as the note says.
57 deaths occurring in 2004 (annual report) and 28 inquests completed January to June 2005 (surveillance report), double counting removed to leave 70; 57 + 28 - 70 = 15 is correct arithmetic.

Both definitions, the 16,088 deaths for 1993 to 2004 (the cited ONS report covers England and Wales) and the 'similar and compact' description in the Discussion's 1st paragraph are at the stated places. In the source, 'with or without a post mortem' qualifies the deaths in which psychoactive substances were implicated; the card's list form is a fair paraphrase.

The rule (known history plus any one of four criteria) and the 'none met' and 'unknown' categories are in the Methods paragraph; Table 1 footnote 1 says only that the classification is np-SAD's, so it supports the attribution, not the rule.
Medians and IQRs, z = 3.942, P < 0.001 and the all-70 median 42.36 (33.28 to 51.35) match; 53.59 - 38.23 = 15.36 years.

19/38, 19/21 (p = 0.002), 7/11 and 45/70 match; non-toxicity deaths 19 + 2 + 4 = 25 of 70 = 35.7%. The drug classes for the toxicity deaths are given in words only (Results; Discussion, 1st paragraph).
All counts, percentages and p-values match Table 1, and footnote 2 says the substances did not necessarily contribute to death.
12/38 and 7/38 against 0/21 (p = 0.005, p = 0.043), 0 in the unknown group, 12/70 = 17.1% and 7/70 = 10.0%; matching on initials, date of birth and sex is in the Methods.
55/70 = 78.6%, so 15 (21.4%) non-residents; group values and p = 0.338 match.

All three cited figures and the proposal are in the Discussion's 2nd paragraph; the authors write 'blood-borne factors'. Add that the 4% comes from a modelling study of people who inject drugs in Scotland (reference 11, Hutchinson et al. 2005), which the authors apply to the UK.

reporting_issues.note: Re-found independently before opening the card. Wording of the consequence: the whole-count figures (17.1%, 10.0%) are a little over half the printed ones (31.6%, 18.4%), so the printed figures are about 85% too high, not 'about half' too high.
Re-found independently: 22/38 = 57.9% against 'half' in the text.

The Background does not say 'regardless of cause': it describes np-SAD as counting 'relevant deaths' where there is a history of drug abuse, without saying which causes count as relevant. Corrected issue: the Background includes deaths with a history of drug abuse (and Table 1 shows 25 of the 70 counted deaths were not from drug toxicity), while the Discussion says np-SAD's definition excludes deaths from bacterial and viral infections; the paper does not reconcile the two. The consequence stands.

Strictly true for cocaine: a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem meets criterion 3, so such a death cannot be classed as not drug abuser/dependent. For treatment and criminal-justice contact it is only partly by construction (substitute prescribing is criterion 2, but linked contact without anything in the coroner's file would not trigger a criterion), so 'expected by construction' in the consequence is a little strong for those two rows.
The ambiguity is mild: the Abstract and the Results both say the categories were assigned by np-SAD. The typographical points are right ('cv.' in the abstract; 'user' in the p-value column heading).

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence with an overall 'moderate' fits a description of what one local count contained. The domain notes are accurate; I confirm the domain 8 statement: each printed p-value reproduces with Fisher's exact test (residence 0.338, methadone 0.022, treatment 0.005, criminal justice 0.043) or the uncorrected chi-square test (sex 0.924, heroin/morphine 0.001, alcohol 0.339, alcohol history 0.569), and toxicity 0.002 and cocaine <0.001 with both. The Wilson intervals (30.0%, 20.5-41.5; 35.6%, 24.6-48.3; 64.3%, 52.6-74.5; 35.7%, 25.5-47.4) and the Newcombe interval (40.5 points, 15.9-57.1) reproduce exactly.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's account of the gap is right, but I would rate it moderate rather than minor. Two statements in the abstract are not results of the data: the Results say the toxicity deaths outside the drug abuser category were mainly from antidepressants, antipsychotics and analgesics, with no counts anywhere in the paper; and the Conclusion says the compact definitions miss deaths from blood-borne viruses, which the study did not examine (it rests on cited figures). The Discussion also calls 21 of 70 deaths 'large numbers'. The main conclusion (the count includes deaths outside np-SAD's drug abuser category) is supported.

missed: Methods name the criminal-justice databases as Drug Arrest Referral 2003/04 and the Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05, but the Table 1 row and footnote 3 cover 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 (Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05 and 2005/06). This minor inconsistency is not recorded, and the card's design_detail gives only the Methods version.

selection_effects says Liverpool had the highest count 'in England and Wales'; the paper says the area of the UK with the highest reported number in 2004 (Background, 2nd paragraph; Abstract, Background).
KF10 / interpretation gap: the 4% cirrhosis figure is from a Scottish modelling study (reference 11), applied by the authors to the UK.
